item.text:
Continuation review round 1 completed for the selected theme `1B`. No score or score range assigned.

The workspace remains read-only, so `research-ledger-manifest.json` could not be updated directly. The append-only entries below are ready for parent persistence, continuing after `E020`.

## New evidence ledger entries

| ID | Canonical claim and precise locator | Source profile and limitations | Lens mapping |
|---|---|---|---|
| E021 | German Basic Law gives the chancellor responsibility for general policy guidelines, primary political responsibility for key decisions, accountability to the Bundestag, and command over the armed forces in a state of defense. Locator: Federal Chancellor duties page, §§158–179. | Official legal/institutional record; high for formal authority. It does not prove day-to-day operational control or unilateral nuclear authority. | 1B.1, 1B.3, 1B.4, 1B.7, 1B.8, 1B.10 |
| E022 | NATO’s Steadfast Noon nuclear exercise ran October 17–30, 2022, involved dozens of aircraft, was described as routine and recurring, and was intended to keep the deterrent “safe, secure and effective.” Locator: NATO release, §§804–816. | NATO official record; high for exercise timing and stated purpose, medium for independent safety assessment. | 1B.2, 1B.3, 1B.7, 1B.8, 1B.10 |
| E023 | In June 2022, the German government stated that NATO nuclear deterrence had to remain credible, selected the F-35 for nuclear-sharing participation, while retaining the goal of a verifiable nuclear-weapons-free world and attending the TPNW meeting as an observer. Locator: Federal Foreign Office press conference, §§160–174. | Official policy record; high for formal position and decision, medium for Scholz-specific ownership because the statement was delivered by Foreign Office officials and referenced Baerbock’s position. | 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.4, 1B.10 |
| E024 | A UN working paper records Germany’s technical support for nuclear verification: surveillance and sealing systems, environmental sampling, nuclear measurement, geospatial analysis, inspection exercises, IAEA equipment and inspector training, and support for impartial technical verification bodies. Locator: UN document, PDF p.3, §§15–16. | UN technical/intergovernmental record; high for documented technical activity, but largely institutional and long-running rather than uniquely Scholz-period. | 1B.3, 1B.4, 1B.7, 1B.9 |
| E025 | Germany’s 2022 G7 presidency supported biological-threat mitigation, BWC implementation, the UN Secretary-General’s mechanism for investigating alleged biological-weapon use, and a Capstone simulation exercise conducted in Germany in September 2022. Locator: Federal Foreign Office declaration, §§106–124. | Official multilateral record; high for formal activity, medium for outcome and individual Scholz attribution. | 1B.7, 1B.9, 1B.10 |
| E026 | A UN BWC working paper gives technical detail: Germany funded UNSGM readiness, supported a September 2022 full-scale biological-weapons investigation exercise, funded reference laboratories, and implemented biosecurity work through the Robert Koch Institute, Bundeswehr Institute of Microbiology, and other institutions. Locator: UN document, PDF p.11, §§53–55. | UN record with technical institutional detail; high for documented implementation, but not evidence of personal Scholz direction. | 1B.3, 1B.7, 1B.9 |
| E027 | Germany’s 2021 Cyber Security Strategy, still operative during 2022, required measurable and transparent targets, critical-infrastructure protection, defined authority allocation, interagency cooperation, periodic review, and implementation monitoring. Locator: Federal Government release, §§121–172. | Official strategy; high for inherited policy architecture, not evidence of a new Scholz-period decision or catastrophic-risk outcome. | 1B.7, 1B.9, 1B.10 |
| E028 | The 2023 National Security Strategy was developed partly in response to the previous 18 months, including Russia’s invasion, and explicitly integrated cyber space, pandemic prevention, critical infrastructure, and broader security policy. Locator: Federal Government retrospective, §§211–238. | Post-period official retrospective; context only for the 2022 process, not a target-year outcome. | 1B.7, 1B.9, 1B.10 |
| E029 | Specialist reporting described Germany’s F-35 decision as specifically linked to NATO nuclear-sharing mechanics; NATO planners were updating planning and exercises around the aircraft, while Germany remained a non-nuclear state and did not control the weapons. Locator: Defense News, §§71–85. | Specialist defense media; medium_high for technical and organizational context, subject to reliance on NATO officials. | 1B.3, 1B.5, 1B.7, 1B.10 |
| E030 | Academic analysis characterizes Germany’s 2022 F-35 procurement as continuation of NATO nuclear-sharing responsibility: Germany does not produce or control nuclear weapons but shares risk and responsibility with allies; the decision reflected confidence in the US extended-deterrence pledge. Locator: De Gruyter article, §§200–202. | Scholarly analysis; medium_high, later publication but directly analyzing the 2022 decision. | 1B.1, 1B.3, 1B.4, 1B.10 |
| E031 | Independent peace-policy analysis argues that the F-35 decision represented nuclear-sharing modernization and a setback for nuclear arms control, despite official German support for eventual nuclear abolition and participation as a TPNW observer. Locator: Toda Peace Institute, §§56–76. | Independent policy institute; medium, useful adverse/contrary interpretation but not a technical finding of unsafe conduct. | 1B.1, 1B.4, 1B.10 |

Locator: Time report, §§4–6 and §§12. | Reputable media; medium_high for chronology and risk context, not evidence that Germany caused unsafe escalation. | 1B.2, 1B.8, 1B.10 |

## Coverage update

The continuation materially improved:

- Formal authority and division of responsibility: E021.
- Nuclear doctrine and nuclear-sharing continuity: E023, E029–E031.
- Exercise evidence and crisis-context risk: E022, E033.
- Technical verification and safeguards: E024.
- Biological-risk governance: E025–E026.
- Cyber-risk governance: E027.
- Independent implementation/adverse evidence: E031, E034.

The source mix now includes official German records, NATO, UN technical material, specialist defense media, academic analysis, an independent peace-policy institute, and general reputable media.

## Remaining gaps

The following could not be responsibly resolved within this bounded continuation:

- Exact German command-and-control arrangements for nuclear-sharing missions, including the practical “dual-key” division between US custody and German aircraft/crew responsibilities.
- Scholz’s personal role relative to the defense minister, Foreign Office, NATO Nuclear Planning Group, Bundestag, and coalition partners in the F-35 decision.
- Classified safeguards, accident-prevention procedures, custody arrangements, and operational readiness findings.
- Independent technical evaluation of Steadfast Noon safety, German participation, or any measurable risk change.
- Target-period AI existential-risk policy. Searches found general German AI and cyber strategies, but no 2022 Scholz-specific policy addressing frontier-AI catastrophic risk.
- Independent outcome evidence showing that the 2022 nuclear-sharing, arms-control, cyber, or biosecurity posture became safer or more dangerous by year-end.

## Local-prior reuse

The supplied local facts remain unchanged and were not re-fetched:

- `LF049` and `LF096` were reused as military-spending context.
- `LS048` and `LS051` were reused as longitudinal spending context.
- No local fact was treated as direct evidence of nuclear command, doctrine, safeguards, or existential-risk responsibility.
- No client-matrix evidence was used.

The 1B dossier is improved but remains attribution-sensitive: the strongest new evidence establishes formal authority, technical institutional activity, nuclear-sharing modernization, and an adverse arms-control interpretation. It still does not establish a complete personal decision chain or independent end-period risk outcome.
